Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(businesslauncher): the package installs, and an extension can finally tell its owner from a stranger

The shop is installable end to end: a front anyone can open without an account, a
back office, the engine that holds stock, and the cortex lib both apps reach it
through. Four components, one call, and the installer's existing reverse rollback
covers all of it.

The apps do not call /v1/ext/ and cannot: an app may only ask for the scopes in
the app-grant vocabulary and there is no `ext:` word in it. Reaching an extension
is cortex's job, so the lib is a real component rather than convenience.

Nothing is seeded into the installer's memory. Products, prices and pages live in
the owner's own organism, and the back office finds that workspace by the
CONTRACT its manifest declares rather than by a stored id. An app cannot create an
organism, so that one step is a prompt the owner runs in their own AI — the same
shape the signage admin uses.

CORE ADDITION, found by the denial-coverage gate rather than by us. The suite was
refused for having no cross-owner case. Writing one showed that a second account
could take over an installed shop: the sandbox had no way to tell its own owner
from any other signed-in stranger, so the only available pattern was "whoever
calls first claims it" — and on a per-owner extension that is a window between
the install and the owner first opening the back office.

`ctx.extension = { name, owner }` now comes from the record (`installedBy`),
resolved server-side and unreachable by anything a caller sends. Every road that
knows the record passes it; a road that does not leaves it absent, and a script
must read that as "not the owner" rather than as permission. The shop's claim step
is gone entirely: it belongs to whoever installed it, from the first second.

The E2E checks the consent claim rather than asserting it: the dry run creates
nothing, the install is ONE call, and the install order is asserted so an app can
never register before the engine whose name it carries. It also proves this
branch's first commit inside a real package — the three crew-defs are on the
installed record, which they would not be against the old registrar.

Gates: e2e-businesslauncher 14/14 and e2e-extensions 32/32 on sqlite and
postgres-kysely, guard tier 455/455 on both, unit 2796/2796, lint and typecheck
clean.

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
test(e2e): the knowledge package that would have exported its private entry to anyone

Part B, batch five, last suite — and the memory group is finished. `src/` is unchanged; all three new
cases were proved by applying the mutation the audit named and watching only them fail.

BOTH SHARING TESTS USED THE ONE PACKAGE THAT HAS NOTHING TO HIDE. "Export a package" and "Clone a
package" both point at `discoverablePackageId`, whose entry list is one PUBLIC entry and nothing else.
So the `.filter(e => e.visibility === 'public')` on each path is never observed: drop both and the
suite is green. The package that matters is the FIRST one imported, which carries a `private-notes`
entry whose body is the string 'Secret stuff' AND `allow_clone: true`.

Export is unauthenticated. With the filter gone, `GET /v1/knowledge/:id/export?format=json` hands that
body to anybody who asks — measured, the string is in the response. The new case exports the first
package and requires the body absent, the entry unlisted, and the public entries still present, so the
absence is a filter rather than an empty export.

Clone copies into the caller's own namespace. The new case reads the cloned ENTRY out of memory at
`packages/{cloned}/private-notes` as the cloner, rather than reading the manifest: a manifest read
depends on the response shape and on the read door's own filtering, and an unauthenticated one would
have hidden a private entry that WAS carried across — which is how the first version of this test
passed under the mutation and had to be rewritten. The public entry is read back as the control.

MODERATION · THE SUITE'S OWN OWNER IS THE OPERATOR. Both admin tests use ownerToken, and that account
is the first owner registered on the cleared database, so it holds the role by bootstrap promotion and
no ordinary owner is ever refused. Delete requireRole('operator') from GET /v1/admin/knowledge and
POST /v1/admin/knowledge/:id/review and node-wide moderation opens to every account with the suite
green. Measured: a plain owner lists every package on the node, 200. The new case registers one,
requires 403 on both doors, and then reads the package's reviews to prove the refused rejection was
not recorded.

MEASURED on both backends: e2e-knowledge and e2e-mcp-knowledge, which share the package store.

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
chore: one line ending for the whole repo, normalised in this commit

This repo had both. 584 of 2864 tracked files were CRLF in their committed blobs and the
rest LF, decided by whichever tool last wrote each file. Nothing read them worse for it,
but any tool that rewrites a file whole — Python's write_text on Windows translates every
newline — turned a one-line edit into a whole-file diff. A 71-line change was committed as
2707 changed lines and a 394-line change as 31,678. The content was correct each time and
the diff was unreviewable.

`.gitattributes` now says `* text=auto eol=lf`, so git normalises at `git add` whatever the
file looks like on disk: the same tool writing the same CRLF now produces no diff at all.
That is the whole fix, and it needs nobody to remember anything.

Two things are declared rather than left to the blanket rule. `*.bat` and `*.cmd` stay CRLF
because Windows shells want them that way on disk. The binary extensions are named
explicitly rather than trusting git's text/binary heuristic, because a false "text" guess
corrupts a file on checkout, and this is not a place to rely on a guess. The two
app-catalog lines that were already in this file are kept as well: `check:app-catalog`
compares a built artifact byte for byte, and an explicit rule outlives a change to the
blanket one.

599 files renormalised here, 158,498 lines, and `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` over the
staged set is EMPTY — not one character of content moved. No binary was touched (no
numstat row went to '-'). The 22 files a parallel session has open right now were skipped
deliberately: they normalise when that session commits them, which is one small diff in
one commit rather than a merge conflict landed on somebody mid-change.

The revision is recorded in .git-blame-ignore-revs, so `git blame` does not point at this
commit for every line in the repo. Enable it per clone with
`git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs`.

Yesterday's answer to this — a pre-commit check that measured the churn and refused it — is
removed in the same commit. With normalisation at `git add` it can never fire, and a gate
that cannot fire is worse than no gate: it reads as protection. The attributes are the
mechanism; the check was a smaller version of the same idea and does not deserve a place in
the hook beside it.

Message:
fix(mcp): an agent writes, and the open page hears about it

Twenty-one of the thirty-one tool files that write emitted no SSE change domain at all. The write
landed, so nothing looked broken — and the person watching the screen saw the old state until they
reloaded, which reads as "the agent did nothing" rather than "the page is stale". It is the quietest
class of drift there is: the board an agent posts to, the task it starts and finishes, the extension
it installs, the cortex it activates, the flag it raises, the sharing group it changes, the work it
accepts and delivers, the morsels an operator mints, the knowledge package it updates, the file it
stores, the membership it ends.

Each emit sits right after its own write, on the success path, and names the domain that
capability's REST twin emits — read from the routes rather than guessed. Where a capability writes
in two steps (deactivate then delete an extension) it announces once, for the act rather than the
step.

surface could reach neither: the change event and the subscriber fan-out. A subscriber is an agent
that asked to be told precisely so it need not poll, so a post made through a tool call was
invisible to every one of them. notifySubscribers is now services/board-subscribers.ts, both it and
the event moved inside createBoardPost, and POST /v1/boards/:id/posts calls that service — so the
post is genuinely one implementation instead of two that agreed on most of it.

server (a token is protocol, not a view), the session layer (it touches the chat instance on every
request, so emitting there would be a frame per tool call), and capabilities (its REST twin emits
nothing either — silence there is parity).

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:

Description: Detected a Generic API Key, potentially exposing access to various services and sensitive operations.
Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
fix(extensions): one sandbox context, and the guards each copy forgot

Four roads reach the extension sandbox: two REST invoke handlers, the MCP
tool, and the scheduler. Each assembled the capability object by hand, about
200 lines apiece, and they were never the same twice. The audit predicted five
findings from that. Measuring while replacing them found eight.

The scheduler wrote memory with no size or key-count limit, so an extension
running on a clock could fill the database while the same extension invoked by
a person could not; the June H-5 fix had landed on two of the three write
paths. The same road fetched with a bare fetch instead of safeFetch, so a
scheduled run had no SSRF guard at all. MCP ran the script without the paywall,
so a priced action was free through a tool call and metered over HTTP. MCP's
wallet had no per-call debit ceiling, which REST has always had. MCP ignored a
script's request for a private memory value and wrote it public. MCP read a
response body by the Content-Type header alone, so a feed that renders
correctly over REST came back as mojibake. The tiered email rule, which decides
whether a sandboxed script may mail a stranger, was typed out three times. And
the scheduler still resolved getPublic with one query per agent, which the
others had long since replaced with one IN.

None of those is hard to see in isolation. All of them are invisible when the
same capability is written four times and a reader has one copy in front of
them.

services/extension-ctx.ts is now the one builder. The guards that must not vary
live inside it: the memory quota, safeFetch, the per-call debit ceiling, the
email authorization rule. What genuinely differs by road is a parameter, and
the difference is stated: a scheduled run has no wallet because nobody's
balance is available to spend on a clock, and notifies the installer because
there is no caller present.

The paywall was Express-shaped, which is why MCP had none of it. enforcePaywall
took an Express Response, the MCP tool has none, so it called nothing.
It now takes a PaywallResponder — status(code).json(body), which an Express
Response already satisfies — and MCP passes a recorder that captures the
refusal and renders it as text. Cross-owner invocation over MCP is intended,
since an extension is a sellable capability and getExtension resolves by name
across owners; the paywall is what makes that safe, and it now runs there too.

The email escape was worse than filed. emailPolicy: 'unrestricted' lifts the
recipient check entirely, and the code reading it has always called that
operator-granted. Nothing enforced it. ext.config comes only from the manifest,
and installing needs requireAuth() plus extInstallRole, which defaults to
owner. So on a node with more than one account, anyone who could install an
extension could send mail to any address under the node's own SMTP identity. A
manifest can no longer set it unless the installer holds the operator role,
which is what the comment always claimed; on a personal node the installer IS
the operator, so nothing changes there.

Three smaller doors closed with it. A manifest can no longer declare the node's
own __-prefixed config keys, which are written from validated manifest
sections. A client-submitted { encrypted: … } value is stripped at the door on
both the manifest and instance paths — no API returns a secret's ciphertext
today, so this closes the door before a backup or a future field opens it, and
removes an invariant that held only because of where the callers happened to
be. And GET /v1/extensions/:name/actions/:actionId now checks installedBy: it
returns scriptContent, the whole implementation of somebody's extension, and
the only thing in front of it was the ext:write scope, which an owner session
bypasses. The PATCH on that exact resource has carried the check all along.

Locked so it cannot drift back. aimeat/no-adhoc-extension-ctx forbids building
the context anywhere else — straight to error with no ratchet, since the four
offenders were fixed in the same change. check:ext-entrypoints gates rather
than reports, and its invariant changed with the code: an entry point takes its
context from the builder and calls enforcePaywall unless it is a road with
nobody to charge, which only the scheduler is.

Also fixed here, from the previous commit: the five audit ratchets went into
the pre-commit hook but not into CI, which --no-verify walks straight past.
check:audit-gates now runs in CI.

Green: 242 E2E on postgres-kysely and sqlite (extensions, paywall, files,
hardening, secrets, MCP, schedules, IAM, pacing, exchange, upsert), 1863 unit
tests, every gate. test/e2e-ext-hardening.ts is new and was proved fail-first:
with the guards disabled, five of its six tests fail, each naming what used to
be possible.

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(memory): merge-patch a record, so several writers can share one key

Approved 2026-08-09. The platform half of letting a multi-writer pipeline consolidate
its keys. Until now the only way to be safe against a concurrent writer was to give
every writer its own key: that is why a six-agent Sanomat edition is 44 keys and why a
collector writes one key per item fetched. Not because the data wants that shape, but
because a read-modify-write through POST /v1/memory is last-write-wins. Remove the race
and the good shape becomes the easy one.

PATCH /v1/memory/:key applies an RFC 7386 merge patch: an object merges key by key,
null DELETES a field, a scalar or array REPLACES. Arrays are never merged element-wise,
because that would make two concurrent appends silently reorder each other. A non-object
patch is refused with 400 rather than replacing the whole record as the RFC would allow:
on a shared record one malformed body would wipe every other writer's subtree.

Safety is read, merge, compare-and-swap, and on a losing swap read again and re-merge,
so a writer that loses the race applies its subtree on top of the winner's rather than
over it. That needed a second storage primitive: setMemoryIfVersion could only UPDATE,
so the FIRST write had nothing to compare against and was still last-write-wins. New
createMemoryIfAbsent (both backends) closes it. Optional if_version gives a caller
explicit CAS; omitted, the route retries instead of failing.

Metadata is patch-like too: omit visibility/tags/ttl and the record keeps what it had.
A writer that owns one subtree has no business restating the whole record's metadata.
Size, quota, reserved-key, data-area and schema checks all run against the MERGED value.

Workflow signals gain a path form of count_nonempty: count the non-empty entries INSIDE
one record instead of counting matching keys. Without it a step that means "at least 12
articles" can only be written as "at least 12 keys matching article.*", so consolidating
those keys breaks the step that verifies the consolidation. Deliberately the same op
rather than a new one, because the watchdog sums count_nonempty leaves to tell "still
filling" from "stuck", and a consolidated pipeline must not lose that.

Not included: the MCP tool. Its two files are held by another session right now.

Gates: lint, typecheck x3, check:openapi (openapi.yaml carries the route). memory-full
(85) and workflows (30) pass on BOTH postgres-kysely and sqlite. 19 new unit tests
across merge semantics (all 15 RFC Appendix A cases), the CAS primitives, and the signal
path form; each proven red first.

A note on the concurrency test: firing six overlapping HTTP patches does NOT prove this
works. Verified by replacing the compare-and-swap with a plain upsert and watching that
test stay green. The primitives are therefore tested by writing the interleave out by
hand: read, read, write, write, assert the second is refused. A test that cannot fail for
the reason it exists is worse than no test, because it reads like coverage.

Two gaps an agent met on connect, neither of which needed a new tool.

The handshake passed no `instructions`, so a client opening /v1/mcp received a few
hundred tool descriptions and nothing saying where to start. The operating guide was

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(provenance): an app builder gets the label without reading the law

Every generative app on this node is, in AI Act terms, a system with a
provider - its owner. Either every builder learns Article 50, or the SDK
hands them the record, one call draws the label, the build prompt asks for
both, the templates ship it wired and publishing checks. Only the second
happens in reality.

AIMEAT.ai.complete() now carries the provenance record through, additively:
it rides in the envelope meta, so `content` and the rest of `data` are
untouched and an app that never heard of provenance keeps working.
disclose() renders the platform badge - the same icon table, the same
stylesheet, inlined at bundle time so there is no SDK copy to drift - and
draws nothing when no label is owed. declare() keeps the record with what
the app stores; chatNotice() covers the first message of a chat.

Publishing warns and never blocks. A publish that fails is a publish that
gets worked around, and the app then ships with less transparency rather
than more; a warning naming the exact call gets the label added. The gap is
recorded on the app and shown to its owner alone.

Two publish doors were found stamping nothing: the presigned upload - the
door most agent-published apps come through - and publish-draft, the one
the catalogue editor uses. The presigned token also erased the acting
agent, keeping only the owner bucket, so there was nothing left to infer
provenance from; it now carries an actor alongside the subject.

Step 0: the four serve-time HTML injectors become one pass, byte-identical
against goldens captured from the old chain, so the last-closing-tag rule
has one home instead of four. Stored files declare charset=utf-8 only after
their bytes pass a UTF-8 decode test - uploaded bytes are not ours to
retype.

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(provenance): the agent path stops losing the record

An agent is not a natural person, so Article 50(1) owes nothing here. This phase
is an engineering duty rather than a legal one: the MCP hop is where provenance
either survives or is lost, and once it is lost no amount of labelling downstream
can reconstruct the truth.

Two ways it was being lost, both found by building rather than by being asked to
look, and both worse than what this phase was scoped to do.

aimeat_memory_write and aimeat_workspace_write went straight to storage. An agent
writing over MCP left content with no provenance at all, while the identical write
over REST was stamped -- so the path that produces most of the content on this
node was the one path that recorded nothing.

And publishing dropped it. The draft carried a record; .latest, which is the copy
a workspace read serves and the label renders from, carried none, on both the REST
and the MCP publish path. Content could be stamped correctly and lose its record
at the moment it became public.

Every write surface now calls the same three functions instead of growing its own
logic: attach an existing record, honour a declaration, fall back to the node's
stamp, in that order. The sentence that only a step where a person reads the
substance and can reject it upgrades human involvement lives in that code, not in
a document nobody reads while writing a workflow step.

Nine write tools accept a declaration and five read tools return the record, so an
agent summarising three items for a person can say which of them a model wrote.
A declaration is checked against the caller's own identity: an agent cannot
attribute its writing to someone else, and the refusal is tested by sending a
false one.

Declaring authorship needs a scope; writing does not. An agent without it still
writes and is stamped honestly, because hiding nine tools from someone who merely
cannot make a claim would trade away their ability to work for a permission the
default does not need.

Served app HTML now declares its charset. Apps have been served as text/html with
no charset since July, so browsers fell back to windows-1252 and any non-ASCII
arrived broken. All 110 published apps were checked first for the one thing that
would make this a regression -- an author who saw the mojibake and compensated --
and none had. The first scan produced a false positive on a Finnish character
class, because a glyph signature cannot tell mojibake from real letters; it was
re-run as a decode test, which can.

The Python connector mirrors the contract. It is not released.

Description: Detected a Generic API Key, potentially exposing access to various services and sensitive operations.
Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(provenance): a provenance record now reaches every surface, and public content can be checked

Phase 1 built the record. It was invisible: every record was minted private and
no surface carried it, so the detection endpoint could only ever find records a
caller had explicitly declared. That is the half that mattered.

Provenance visibility now follows the content. The AiProvenance table's own
visibility column is gone -- deleted, not synced -- and the question "is this
record's subject readable by an anonymous visitor right now" is answered as one
SQL predicate per provider, reused by both the hash lookup and the id resolve so
the two cannot drift apart. Publish content and its record becomes resolvable;
make it private again and it returns to the identical 404. There is no flag a
caller could set to publish a statement about content nobody may read.

memory.visibility is untouched and is what the predicate asks. The record was
denied its own competing visibility concept precisely because the platform
already has one that works.

The predicate runs in SQL rather than in the route. On the anonymous detection
path a third party's non-public row never enters the process, so there is nothing
there for a later mistake to leak.

One place emits the marks: the envelope's meta.provenance, the AI-Disclosure and
Link headers, the serve-time HTML block and the markdown frontmatter all come
from one module, and no external vocabulary string is spelled there -- it all
comes from the adapters.

An agent writing without declaring anything is now recorded as having written it,
because silence from an agent must not read as "a human wrote this". An owner
writing on their own token is not stamped.

Two fixes from the Phase 1 audit ride along. Content a human wrote and a model
edited, on a public page with nobody checking what the model did, now carries a
light label: the letter of Article 50(4) says otherwise, but we decided to
over-label and the EU's own icon set has a category defined for exactly that
case. And attestation.observed can only ever be narrowed -- it was being derived
from who stamped the record, so a node-stamped inference was being recorded as an
observation. The record was overstating its own strength.

/v1/ai-transparency states what this node marks and how. It reports the AI
market-surveillance authority as unknown rather than borrowing the data
protection one, which is a different authority and would have been a false
statement in a compliance artefact.

code-style.md gains the naming section it never had: camelCase internally,
snake_case on the wire mapped at the route, and one spelling for self-describing
documents that carry their own spec. That rule was real, consistent, and written
down nowhere.

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(provenance): content the node generates can say how it was made

EU AI Act Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026. It asks two things of anyone
publishing what a model wrote: tell a person, and mark it so a machine can tell.
This is the substrate for the second half. Nothing is visible yet.

One record, aimeat.provenance/v1: what level of AI involvement, how much a human
was involved, which model, which principal, when, and a SHA-256 of the exact
bytes it is a statement about. Four fields are required so a caller can always
produce a valid record; minting fills everything the node knows for free.

Minted at the one place completions already pass through, so there is no second
path to keep in sync. The ledger event gains an optional link to what the spend
produced.

The five external vocabularies (IPTC, the W3C attribute, the IETF header, the EU
icon, a C2PA assertion) are produced by pure adapter functions and never stored.
Four of them disagree with each other already; two come from the same proposal
family and still disagree. Storing one would mean inheriting its future.

Records are append-only. A correction is a new record about new bytes, not an
edit to a statement someone may have already read.

/v1/provenance/by-hash/:sha256 answers without an account for public content.
That is deliberate: it is the detection access point the Code of Practice asks
for by February 2027, and building it behind auth first is the retrofit this
design exists to avoid. /v1/provenance/:id returns the same 404 for "no such
record" and "not yours", so it cannot be used to probe what exists.

The four `level` strings had two definitions before this; now they have one, and
the knowledge package references it.

Description: Detected a Generic API Key, potentially exposing access to various services and sensitive operations.
Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(exchange): a provider can share what they earn with third parties

Settlement knew exactly two commercial parties plus the platform rake, so
"and N % of this goes to a third account" had nowhere to live. This adds a
SECOND RAKE, shaped like the first: the platform rake takes a percent of what
the consumer pays and routes it to one operator account; this takes a percent
of what the PROVIDER earns and routes it to N beneficiary GHIIs by weight.

The pocket is the whole argument. A share carved out of the buyer's charge
would invent a contract they never signed, bill them twice for one purchase,
and put the VAT chain the wrong way round. A share carved out of the
provider's own cut is the provider giving away their own revenue, which needs
nobody's permission but theirs. So the provider is paid their whole cut at
settlement and separately owes a share onward, and the node holds nothing at
any instant, on either rail. That last part is why the morsel rail works too:
a withheld morsel pool would be custody in morsel terms.

Who shares it comes from two places. A standing declaration on the coordinate
covers the ordinary case; a capability may also name destinations per call by
returning `_revenue: { beneficiaries: [...] }`, which the node reads, resolves
and strips before the buyer sees it. It names destinations ONLY: the pool
percent is server-held config read at settlement, so a capability can redirect
a share its provider already committed and can never enlarge its own payout.
It is read off provider output, never a request body.

Accruing and paying are separated deliberately. Accrual is unconditional and
must never block a call, wait on paperwork, or vanish; release refuses until
an operator records a verified approval, which lives in a system namespace no
principal can write and defaults to unverified BY ABSENCE. Paying a party
nobody checked is how a self-declared claimant collects on someone else's
identity.

Rounding conserves by construction: the pool floors so a provider never
over-pays their declared percent, then divides by largest remainder so the
lines sum to it exactly. price === platformFee + providerNet + shares, proven
over adversarial amounts rather than inferred from a ledger.

accrue() rides on the settled outcome beside refund() so every door calls
exactly one of them and no second chokepoint appears; all five doors wired.

Not split: the uncontracted raw-call channel, which settles outside
settleMeteredCharge and would need a second copy of the arithmetic.

Unit 18/18. E2E 30/30 on PostgreSQL+Kysely and SQLite. Full sweep 3965/3976
on both, the 11 failures pre-existing and unrelated (oauth env, x402 testnet,
SMTP, a stale header-nav fixture).

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(commerce): pacing moves to the chokepoint every metered call shares

Morsels and money do two different jobs. Money moves value to the provider. Morsels regenerate on a
daily allowance with a hard ceiling, so burning them per call puts an absolute floor under how fast a
capability can be consumed — the one property money does not have. A runaway loop against a money-priced
capability drains a budget at machine speed and stops only when the money runs out.

The toll that does this lived inside `enforcePaywall`, which guards exactly one of four metered paths:
raw extension invokes. App-tool calls, exchange runs, agent work and the MCP run tools all reach
settlement through `settleMeteredCoordinate` directly and were paced by nothing at all. That was not a
decision — the paywall was written on 2026-07-17 when extension invokes were the only metered surface,
the shared gateway arrived three days later with EXCHANGE, and nobody moved the toll across.

Now the burn lives in `pacing.ts` and happens once per call, either inside the chokepoint (contracted
calls, any unit) or on the uncontracted path — the paywall consults the entitlement gate first, so a
single call can never pay it twice. It is charged BEFORE the price, so a paced-out call leaves nothing
to refund, and it stays a burn: the provider is never credited (invariant M1) and an owner calling their
own capability is not paced.

The amount is the value pinned on the entitlement at accept when the capability declared one, else the
node's `AIMEAT_PACING_TOLL_DEFAULT`. Pacing is a property of the node, not of each seller's memory.
The default ships as 0: raising it changes what existing consumers are charged, which is an operator's
decision, not a silent upgrade. At 1 a consumer can make roughly 500 calls a day against anything.

New e2e-pacing suite (self-spawns a node with the default on, because the default IS the feature):
a money contract is paced, the toll is a burn the provider never receives, an owner is exempt, and a
runaway loop against a 100 EUR budget dies on the morsel ceiling with the budget barely touched.
5/5 on SQLite and PostgreSQL+Kysely; e2e-extensions 31/31, e2e-commerce 34/34, e2e-exchange-projection
20/20. e2e-x402 is 16/16 against a test facilitator; the four failures on the shared runner are the
real facilitator rejecting synthetic signatures, verified identical before this change.

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(mcp): commerce over MCP — PSP (masked), app-tool manifests, offer pricing, checkout (TARGET-033/034)

Agents can now manage their own selling and buy over the MCP surface —
9 new tools wrapping EXISTING commerce mechanisms (the commerce.psp /
apps.{appId}.tools memory-record conventions the sellable resolvers read,
the agents.{name}.offers document via the same OffersDocSchema as REST,
and src/commerce/session-service.ts). No new business logic.

Tools + scopes (registered per-session against the agent's scope snapshot;
catalog/scopes.ts documents that these are deliberately STRICTER than the
requireAuth-only REST commerce routes — PSP secrets + owner-balance
spending warrant least-privilege on the agent surface):
  commerce:sell — aimeat_commerce_psp_set / _status / _delete (the secret
    is stored private under the owner GHII and NEVER returned; status is
    provider + last-4 hint), aimeat_app_tools_publish (schema-validated,
    public record, returns skus + call|task fulfillment), and
    aimeat_offer_price_set (morsels and/or priceMoney in 6-decimal
    micro-units via money.ts; whole doc revalidated with OffersDocSchema;
    own agents only — the GAII is built from the session owner).
  commerce:buy — aimeat_checkout_open / _complete / _list over the shared
    session service. checkout_complete mints a 120s JWT for the CALLING
    agent itself (issueJWT re-issuance, no privilege lift) so callable
    app-tool fulfillment can authenticate its capability invoke — the MCP
    layer holds no forwardable bearer.
  ungated — aimeat_app_tools_get (public manifests; own always; a foreign
    private manifest is indistinguishable from missing).

aimeat_admin_config (operator-only) now also reads the commerce/readiness
posture (commerce_enabled, mcp_card_commerce_tools, content_signal,
web_bot_auth_sign) — READ-only there because those are boot-time env
config (robots.txt baked + Web Bot Auth signer armed at startup); a
runtime setter would silently no-op until restart.

NOT wrapped (documented): /v1/orgs/:slug/psp + company KYB — the whole
/v1/orgs namespace is Enterprise-edition (community stub answers 501
ENTERPRISE_REQUIRED) and its logic lives behind the provider seam with its
own REST auth; the MCP layer holds no forwardable credential, and minting
one to impersonate the caller against EE routes would create a
token-forging primitive. EE can contribute its own MCP tools via a future
provider seam instead.

Catalog: definitions/commerce.ts (+ definitions.ts), scopes.ts
(commerce:sell/buy), surfaces.ts (agent: buyer tools; service: all nine),
annotations.ts (checkout_complete flagged destructive+openWorld).

E2E: new e2e-mcp-commerce 12/12 on SQLite AND MongoDB — scope-filtered
surface (narrow memory-only agent sees only the ungated read), PSP
set/status/delete with secret-never-echoed + private-record assertions,
manifest publish landing in /v1/commerce/tools, offer priced 1_500_000
micros EUR + persisted, and a cross-owner app-tool purchase completed
end-to-end over MCP (fee arithmetic on both wallets + the seller task
carrying the buyer input). Neighboring suites unchanged: e2e-mcp 40/40,
mcp-scopes 4/4, mcp-v2 8/8, commerce 34/34. openapi.yaml untouched (MCP
is not the REST contract; no REST routes added).

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(messages): send-as-owner delegation so AI can reply as you (TARGET-031)

Adds a consent-gated delegation behind Inbox \"Reply with AI\": a new MCP tool
aimeat_dm_send_as_owner lets the owner\x27s own agent post a Postilaatikko reply AS
THE OWNER, into the owner\x27s thread, so the recipient sees it from the human -
not from the agent (which was the bug: aimeat_dm_send always sends as the agent
identity, landing in a separate thread + the recipient\x27s requests).

Safety (Rule 10): the sender is derived SERVER-SIDE from the calling agent\x27s own
GAII, so an agent can only ever speak as its OWN owner - never cross-owner (there
is no owner parameter to spoof). Gated by a new messages:send-as-owner scope; the
tool is only on the surface when the agent holds it (part of the full * bundle;
granular agents opt in via the Agents tab). The acting agent is logged for audit.

- MCP: aimeat_dm_send_as_owner registered across scopes/surfaces/definitions/
  annotations; handler derives owner via parseGaiiLoose and calls sendDirectMessage.
- UI: messages:send-as-owner added to the Agents-tab scope catalog (+ en/fi label
  \"Reply as me\").
- Prompt: Reply-with-AI MCP mode now uses aimeat_dm_send_as_owner with a graceful
  fallback to hand the reply back when the scope is not granted; never aimeat_dm_send.
- E2E test/e2e-dm-send-as-owner.ts (7/7): tool-gating by scope, sends as owner into
  the owner thread, recipient sees the human, no-scope blocked, own-owner-only.

MCP-only (no REST route) so no openapi change.

Message:
feat(mcp): Phase 3 — per-agent scope enforcement on /v1/mcp (F1)

Close the least-privilege hole where /v1/mcp registered all tools for every agent regardless of granted scopes. createMcpServer now reads the agent's defaultScopes and filters the registered tool surface via catalog/scopes.ts:scopeAllowsTool() (wildcard semantics mirror auth/middleware.ts: global *, domain:*, exact).

Only tools whose REST route is genuinely requireScope-gated are gated on MCP too (memory/social/wallet/work/consent) — so MCP stays consistent with REST and agents lose only what REST already 403s. Ungated tools (tasks, apps, extensions, organisms, knowledge, storage, catalogue, public board reads, onboarding) stay available. Admin tools remain runtime operator-gated. A '*' scope (owner-attached / Claude Desktop) sees the full surface.

AIMEAT_MCP_ENFORCE_SCOPES (default true) toggles warn-only rollout (register all, log would-be-filtered). scope-profiles map AgentRecord.mode to existing-scope bundles for provisioning.

Verified: typecheck, lint 0 errors, 9 scopes unit tests, new e2e-mcp-scopes (4) + 219 MCP e2e sweep (SQLite). Connector already enforces via REST 403; register-time connector filtering deferred (UX only).

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(atelier): the mosaic server — component registry, worded validator, versioned layouts, three doors

TARGET-074 phase 2: "move the numbers above the list" becomes one read and
one write instead of an edit-and-publish round.

The app-ui registry (src/services/app-ui/) declares eleven mosaic components
as DATA on the same typed prop grammar the surface-layout blocks use —
surface-layout's propProblem judge is now exported and shared, so the two
registries can never grow different validation rules for the same idea. One
declaration derives the validator, the catalogue every read answers with
(components, settings, the five navigation modes, the seven looks), and the
seam the gallery and the client renderer will hang from.

The validator refuses with words AND — new against the surface-layout
precedent, which only enumerates — suggests the NEAREST REAL NAME when a
component, setting, look or nav mode is a typo away ("cardgird — did you
mean cardGrid?"). One hero per layout (two focal points is shouting), a
required setting names its own description when missing, and a hero image
data: URI is refused with the storage remedy in the answer.

One app's layout is a memory record in its owner's namespace
(atelier.mosaic.<filename>): whole-value replace, archived on overwrite, so
undo is one restore call and the set tool needs no undo machinery. Reads are
as public as the app (the app page fetches its layout without a session);
writes resolve the caller to an owner and refuse everyone else naming whose
layout it is. Trusted-keys carries the reviewed reason this is user data by
design, not server-acted configuration — and the ratchet turned: one stale
exemption out, this one in.

Three doors from day one: REST (catalogue, dry-run validate as a 200-worded
RESULT, ui get/put/versions/restore — all scope-gated, zero new entries in
the route-scope ratchet), node MCP (aimeat_app_ui_get/set through the same
service — the no-storage-in-mcp lint pushed the ownership decision into the
service, where it now exists exactly once), connector proxy and the CLI
dispatch. The pair joins audit-mcp-schemas' capture list on arrival — the
measurement found the surface-layout pair had been left outside that gate,
and outside the gate is where drift lives. No new scope word: the layout is
memory, so memory:read/memory:write gate it.

A layout's titles and wording are text a person reads, so the write is
stamped like any other: the set tool takes the standard ai_provenance
declaration on all three doors, the service mints the record against the
layout's own bytes (declared if the caller said something, Mint-3 if it said
nothing), and aimeat_app_ui_set joins the disclosure gate's required list —
the gate itself refused this commit until the decision was made, which is
the gate working.

e2e-app-ui: 18 cases, refusals first — did-you-mean on components, settings
and looks, the hero cap, the data:-URI remedy, 401/403-by-name, the
untouched-layout-after-refusal proof, whole replace, history and restore.
18/18 on both backends; guard tier 509/509 on both; openapi documents all
six paths in the same commit.

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(data-map): the map an AI reads before it touches an app you did not write

The first version answered nobody's question. It rendered a key pattern and its
compliance columns on seven surfaces and never said what the app was FOR, so the rows
were a list nobody could judge. And when an app said nothing it DERIVED a map from the
permission words, which put the same confident row on 114 apps — `kansi.*`, "you named
it", "nobody has said why this is here" — sitting exactly where the answer belonged and
reading like one. `kansi.html` has never written a key under `kansi.`; it uses
`julkaisu.`. The guess was not incomplete, it was wrong, and it was wrong everywhere.

The definition is now written down, in the words it was agreed in:
docs/datakartta-maaritelma.md. Two levels. The app level says what this app IS, what it
is USED FOR, what shape it is, how its data is actually arranged, what machinery it
leans on and what leaves the house. The row level says, per key family: what it holds,
what kind of thing it is, what it is used for, where it lives, who owns it, who reads
it, who writes it, what shape the record is, how long it is kept, whether losing it
matters, and one sentence saying why it is there rather than somewhere else.

The two fields that carry the value cannot be derived and are written once, by whoever
built the app: the paragraph and the per-row `why`. So the node stopped guessing. An app
with no map is stamped `missing`, which is the honest answer and the one that gets a map
written. `data-map-derive.ts`, `data-map-lint.ts`, `data-map-meta.ts`,
`form-requirements.ts` and the backfill script are gone with the guessing they served.

And the thing that was missing entirely: nothing anywhere told an app-building AI to
write one. The parser read a declaration nobody made. build-app-prompt.ts now carries
the instruction, the shape, the closed vocabulary and the three rules that decide
whether a map is worth anything — including "leave a `why` you do not know EMPTY",
because a plausible wrong one is believed and acted on.

The one check that pays for the whole feature: an app that says several people share it,
whose every row lands in one person's own memory, is flagged on sight. That is CADENCE's
original defect — campaigns, deal stages, follow-up limits and IAM binding all in one
person's private memory, invisible to their team — and it is now readable from two
columns without opening the source. It renders panel-wide in body text above everything
else, and the list line says DOES NOT ADD UP so it is visible without opening anything.

Two surfaces, not seven. Profile › Apps shows one line per app and OPENS IN PLACE — it
used to throw you into the app catalogue, a different page with a different job. The
catalogue detail shows the whole map. Extensions, packages, agents, the ecosystem tab
and the Data Wallet coverage list are all out: a map describes an APP, and that list
inventoried the whole keyspace, which answers nothing for somebody about to work on one
thing.

Verified in a browser at 390x844, 1280x900 and 1280x460 with a real map written from
CADENCE's own skill: no horizontal overflow at any width, every column on one x per
viewport, the line opens in place without navigating, all three states distinguishable
in a 36-app list (1 written, 1 contradicted, 34 with no map), and the contradiction
banner measured at body size and 911 of 945 panel pixels. Test data removed: two probe
apps and their two map records.

Gates: lint, typecheck, typecheck:frontend, check:importmap, check:locales,
check:plain-language, check:openapi, check:app-catalog, check:mcp-tools,
check:mcp-schemas, check:trusted-keys (one stale exemption removed, the ratchet turns),
vitest 2985, e2e-data-map 10/10 on both backends, guard tier 501/501 on both.

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(data-map): the publish stamp, on the terms the AI posture already set

TARGET-073 step 6. Publishing an app now drafts where it puts what, stamps the summary on
the manifest beside aiPosture, and hands the findings back in the response. All four doors
say the same thing: POST /v1/apps, publish-draft, and both MCP publish tools.

The map itself is a public memory record at apps.{appId}.datamap, written through
writeMemoryRecord and never storage.setMemory -- the shortcut that is exactly how the tool
manifest came to skip the archive guard, the value ceiling, the key ceiling and the
provenance stamp. The manifest carries the SUMMARY only, because the rows carry a sentence
each and prose does not belong on a blob every listing loads.

The rows are public and the gap is not, which is the same split publicPosture() makes.
Where an app puts data is the promise it makes to whoever installs it, and an agent
deciding whether to use it needs that before it touches anything; the publish check's
finding is the owner's own unfinished business.

THE E2E ASSERTS AT EVERY DOOR THAT NOTHING IS REFUSED, because that is the decision and a
decision that lives only in a comment is one somebody tightens later by accident.

Two model errors the E2E caught, both of which would have fired on the ordinary case:

An app that writes and cannot delete was getting "deletion: unknown". Wrong: the record is
in the OWNER'S store, so the owner's delete removes it whether or not the program was
granted memory:delete -- that permission says who can press the button, not what the button
does. As written it would have reported a missing deletion answer for 73 of 168 production
apps, which is a finding that fires on the normal case and teaches people to ignore
findings.

And a wholly DERIVED map was being held to a declared map's standard, so it failed the form
check and the why check at once. A draft has no author yet. The three findings that are
about a statement somebody made are now asked only of the rows somebody wrote, and the one
true thing to say about a draft -- nobody has confirmed this -- is what gets reported. On
day one every app has a derived map, so getting this wrong meant three misleading findings
each on 169 apps.

The trusted-key gate wanted its exemption and got a real one, including the caveat it
deserves: a generic memory:write app grant lands in the owner namespace and can reach
apps.*, so a granted app can write a false map for another of that owner's apps. Nothing
routes, authorises, prices or refuses on the value, and the comparison against the declared
permissions reports the forgery as a contradiction rather than acting on it.

openapi.yaml carries DataMapStamp and both new response fields in this commit; types
regenerated.

The denial-coverage gate then refused the commit, and it was right: the suite drove one
principal and proved the feature without proving any fence. The first refusal written for it
asserted the wrong one -- a cross-OWNER write -- and passed with a 201, because memory is
keyed by whoever wrote it and there is no cross-owner write path to refuse. The fence that
actually exists is the scope: the map is a memory record, so writing one needs memory:write,
and a read-only agent of the same owner is refused 403.

Verified: e2e-data-map 8/8 on BOTH backends, e2e-apps 61/61, e2e-app-ai-posture 13/13,
e2e-app-publish-gate 19/19, e2e-app-fork 34/34, guard tier 501/501 on both backends, 2983
unit tests, lint, typecheck, check:openapi, check:trusted-keys, check:mcp-tools,
check:mcp-schemas, check:plain-language.

One thing left alone: the gate reports a stale exemption for
src/services/living-pulse.ts:organism. that matches no read any more. Not mine, and the
honest reasons differ -- a read that moved and a read that vanished want different fixes.

Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(signals): the node can count what was reached, once, for every channel

A customer asked whether CADENCE could send one message to a chosen set of contacts and then
show who opened it and who clicked, the way HubSpot does. The sending half already exists (the
outbound door, its recipient registry, opt-out and per-company SMTP). The measuring half did not
exist anywhere, and building it inside one app would have meant building it again for the next
one.

So this is a capability, not a feature: an email open, a link click, a published-page fetch, a QR
scan and an app's own event all land in ONE record shape, and a report can hold them side by side.
Cadence is its first consumer, and owns none of it.

THE SHAPE IS ONE KEY PER STREAM PER MONTH, which is the decision everything else hangs off. The

Description: Detected a Generic API Key, potentially exposing access to various services and sensitive operations.
Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(company-brain): a company that remembers, installable in one step (TARGET-071)

Installing "company-brain" gives an owner three components under their own identity: the brain,
the sandboxed caretaker that keeps its source register honest, and the cortex lib between them.

IT KNOWS WHICH COMPANY IT IS FROM THE ADDRESS IT IS SERVED AT. On {slug}.co.<apex> the first
label of the host IS the company slug, and one pass over GET /v1/companies turns it into the
record. That is what lets one owner install this once per company with no configuration channel
at all -- and there is none: install takes version, label and dry_run, and none of the three
reaches a component. The address is the parameter.

THE REGISTERED DETAILS ARE THE FIRST FACTS. Setup turns each FILLED IN company field into an
anchored fact pointing back at the entry the owner wrote themselves. Anchored means it never
falls due, because the document is theirs. An empty field produces no fact: it is something
nobody has told this company yet, not knowledge with a blank value. Measured in the browser:
eight filled fields, eight facts, four blanks, nothing.

AGEING IS DECIDED WHEN THE PAGE RENDERS. An observed fact carries review_after and is compared
with today in the browser. Nothing sweeps facts: it costs nothing, cannot drift and has no job
to notice it broke. What DOES need a clock is a feed that has gone quiet, because silence leaves
no record of itself, and that is the caretaker's one job -- a `kind: extension` schedule with no
model call in it, so the weekly check spends no tokens and needs no key of the owner's.

THE SOURCE REGISTER LIVES IN THE EXTENSION, not the workspace, and that is forced rather than
chosen: a sandboxed extension reads an owner's memory only where it is PUBLIC, so a register
kept in the workspace would be invisible to the one job that exists to check it. It also belongs
there on its own merits -- which feed runs and when it last delivered is machinery, while the
facts it produces are the company's knowledge and stay in the owner's own workspace where they
can be exported. Every record it writes is private: an ext namespace is world-readable by
default, and a company's list of what it does not know is not a public document.

EVERY SOURCE SAYS WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER, the row renders even when the source has produced
nothing, and the caretaker NAMES any source whose coverage note is empty rather than counting
it. A source whose limits are unwritten is the one that quietly becomes "everything we know".

There is no memory component. Those write to author-chosen keys with no per-instance id, so a
second install would overwrite the first one's records while its app duplicated -- and one
install per company is the whole point, so the failure would be certain rather than latent.

Also in: the playbook that walks it (a NEW prompt id, since prompt-seeder re-syncs content only
for three groups and editing a live playbook never reaches a node that has seeded it), a fourth
chat starter -- the other three name something the PERSON does, this names something their
company gets -- and en/fi/es for both.

test/e2e-company-brain.ts, 17 cases: the package ships with the node, installs, rewrites the
app's short names to this instance's, a second install shares no component name with the first,
and the caretaker's verdicts are asserted rather than trusted (never delivered is late, an error
is broken, a one-off import is neither, forever). Plus the fences: a stranger is refused, the
register is unreadable without a session, and installing needs packages:write by name.

Description: Detected a Generic API Key, potentially exposing access to various services and sensitive operations.
Author: Jouni Miikki
Message:
feat(sso): an organisation connects its own identity provider (BR-04)

SAML 2.0 sign-in, SCIM 2.0 provisioning and the account state the platform
never had: deactivated. An organisation's directory now decides who signs in
here and, when someone leaves, everything acting in their name stops within
the same request while their knowledge stays theirs.

WHAT SHIPS

- Owner deactivation (services/owner-lifecycle.ts): OwnerRecord gains
  disabledAt/disabledBy/managedBy on both backends (PG migration 0047 +
  sqlite safeAddColumn). The flag is written first, then every credential
  family ends: sessions (owner, agents, ecosystem apps), PATs, app grants,
  in-flight device auths, MCP OAuth refresh tokens, live connect-tunnel
  sockets (new ConnectTunnelManager.closeForOwner). credentialRevoked() asks
  it as its FOURTH question on every authenticated request (federated
  principals excluded — their home node refuses the attestation instead),
  resolvePat() answers null, and issueJWT() itself refuses to mint for a
  deactivated local owner, so a door that forgot to ask still cannot mint.
  Cost measured on postgres-kysely: getOwner mean 0.36 ms, p95 0.54 ms.
  Operator doors: POST /v1/admin/owners/:name/disable|enable (+ admin UI,
  + MCP tools); never on yourself; SCIM can never deactivate an operator.

- SSO connections (storage table sso_connections on both backends, PG 0048):
  one record per organisation — email domains, optional organism its people
  join on arrival, the SAML half read from IdP metadata (URL via safeFetch or
  pasted XML), the SCIM bearer shown once and stored as SHA-256. Managed at
  runtime by an operator through /v1/admin/sso (routes), the admin dashboard's
  Organisation sign-in tab (five-step playbook where every step shows what the
  node has actually SEEN, plus Entra/Okta walkthroughs, troubleshooting and a
  copyable brief for the operator's own AI), and nine aimeat_admin_sso_* /
  aimeat_admin_owner_* MCP tools on all three surfaces — every one calling
  the single implementation in services/sso-connections.ts. The freeze
  (sso.connections_locked) and the master switch (sso.enabled) are ordinary
  runtime config keys an organisation node's host SEALS with
  AIMEAT_SEALED_CONFIG_KEYS — deliberately not a new immutable env flag.

- SAML login (routes/saml-login.ts over services/saml-sp.ts, a thin wrapper
  on @node-saml/node-saml >=5.1.0 — XML-DSig validation is never ours,
  CVE-2025-54419 is the reason for the version pin): per-connection
  authorize → ACS → finalize, same three-door shape as OIDC and the same
  account-mapping tree, extracted as a PURE MOVE from routes/oauth-login.ts
  into services/external-login.ts (the existing 18-test oauth-login unit
  suite passes unchanged). Mapping order: NameID → the connection's SCIM
  externalId (a provisioned account is ADOPTED, never duplicated) →
  verified email fenced to the connection's own domains → the one-time
  username-choice step under the registration mode. IdP-initiated responses
  are refused unless the connection opts in; wantAuthnResponseSigned is off
  because Entra signs the assertion only, which stays mandatory. Listed
  connections appear as sign-in buttons; hidden ones never reach the public
  modal, so a shared node does not publish its customer list.

- SCIM (routes/scim.ts + services/scim-users.ts on SCIMMY + scimmy-routers,
  chosen after a spike proved Express 5, per-connection context and the
  filter/PATCH machinery; the one thing SCIMMY refuses — Entra's non-RFC
  string booleans — is normalised by a shim with its own unit test):
  /v1/scim/v2/:id/Users with its OWN credential family. requireScimConnection
  resolves the bearer's hash to a connection record and compares the RECORD's
  id to the path; it never touches req.auth, and it is a named gate in
  check-route-scopes. Users only (R8). Creation goes through provisionOwner
  via 'provisioning' (new rule-table row: only `closed` refuses) and NEVER
  triggers the first-owner→operator self-heal — a directory sync cannot
  crown a node's operator. The original userName/externalId are stored
  verbatim so Entra's `filter=userName eq <UPN>` matches. DELETE and
  active:false deactivate; nothing is erased.

TWO PRE-EXISTING HOLES CLOSED ON THE WAY (the deactivation promise does not
hold without them, found by the plan's adversarial review):
- src/mcp/index.ts asked only isRevoked(token): a revoked session or app
  grant kept working over MCP, and the session-resume branch asked nothing.
  Now verifyJWT + credentialRevoked above the resume branch.
- routes/federation-auth.ts attested a password login without reading the
  owner record, so deactivation would not have held on other nodes.
Also: AIMEAT_ENTRA_* was the one provider family not pinned in the E2E
server env, so a developer's .env leaked a live client into tests — pinned.

TESTS, and which of §19's three each green was:
- test/unit/saml-assertion.test.ts (13): the cryptographic refusals against
  REAL signed responses from the embedded fake IdP — all six valid-path
  cases failed first (node-saml's default demanded a signed Response
  envelope; the suite forced the wantAuthnResponseSigned decision).
- test/unit/scim-entra-compat.test.ts (7): asserts the shim it shipped with;
  the raw string-boolean 400 was observed in the spike first.
- test/e2e-owner-deactivation.ts (19): failed 3 first — sqlite's
  methods/owner.ts is a second copy of repos/owner.ts and dropped the new
  columns; the suite caught it, both copies now carry them.
- test/e2e-saml-login.ts (12), test/e2e-scim-users.ts (13): the closed-mode
  case failed first (SCIMMY maps unknown handler errors to 404; domain
  errors are now translated to SCIM errors). All three suites joined
  GUARD_SUITES: every assertion is a refusal or an isolation boundary.
- Guard tier: 501/501 on sqlite AND postgres-kysely. Full vitest: 2878
  passed. Targeted: registration-mode 10/10, oauth-login 10/10, mcp 41/41,
  access-tokens 19/19, agent-onboarding 70/70. e2e-admin-features has one
  pre-existing red (keyed_browse key absent from config-schema at the base
  commit; unrelated, left alone).
- Browser verification (Playwright MCP, three viewports, repaint + idle-net
  counters): the full chain ran in a real browser — connection created in
  the tab, metadata pasted, token minted (shown once), SCIM-provisioned user
  signed in through a signed SAML response and was ADOPTED, the profile
  Security tab names the managing organisation, Owners tab deactivates and
  reactivates. The counters caught a real refetch loop in the new tab
  (load-callback depended on a per-render function; hundreds of requests in
  20 s) — fixed to 0 repaints / 0 requests in 20 s, 60 s idle shows only the
  SPA's build heartbeat. A second real find: the client's overview shaping
  dropped managed_by, so the Security-tab row never rendered — fixed.

DEPENDENCIES (all MIT, pnpm audit clean): @node-saml/node-saml 5.1.0 (the
SAML SP; hand-rolling XML-DSig is where signature-wrapping bugs live),
@xmldom/xmldom (IdP metadata parsing), scimmy + scimmy-routers (SCIM
protocol; last release 2025-03 but the repo is active in 2026, accepted for
a stable protocol), dev xml-crypto (the fake IdP signs test responses).

Left deliberately out (BR-04 scope): /Groups, multi-provider certification,
group-based permission inheritance. openapi.yaml documents every new route
in this commit; locales carry en+fi+es, composed per language.

Every other name has a row: 114 new or reclassified rows in config-schema-runtime.ts, -access.ts, -features.ts and the rate-limit group, with names and descriptions in en, fi and es. A new row kind, `applies: 'restart'`, is stored in the database and takes effect at the next start, for a setting the code reads once at start; PUT stores it without touching the running value and the tab says the node runs with the old value until it restarts. Each new row's readers were read: 37 take effect at once, the sign-in providers, the package, template, payment and e-invoice switches, the message retry interval, the screenshot job and the calibrator wait for the restart. The setup route no longer writes AIMEAT_LOCALE; the language stays on the operator's account.

Message:
fix(security): log redaction, upstream and 500 error text, one-time secrets in the idempotency cache, and the admin backup

Secrets audit 2026-10-09, builder D: findings d1, d4, d5 (07-side-channels), 1.8 and 1.9.

Logger (d1). src/utils/logger.ts masked eight exact lowercase field names at the top level only, so Authorization, apiKey, access_token, client_secret, a nested headers.authorization and a Bearer inside a message or an error string reached the log. The masking is now case-insensitive and recursive (bounded depth, cycle-safe, nested objects copied so the caller's object is not changed), covers the common credential field names and their suffixes (scimToken, webhookSecret, x-api-key), and scrubs key-shaped text in every string: Bearer values, name=value pairs, sk-/sk_live_/sk_test_/whsec_/rk_ and other vendor prefixes, the node's own aimeat_pat_/aimeat_scim_ tokens, JWTs, AES-GCM ciphertext, and token/code/key/state query values. The rules moved from services/ai/errors.ts (redactKeyShaped, re-exported there unchanged) to src/utils/redact-credentials.ts, so the logger uses them without importing a service. The log variant leaves ids, digests and UUIDs readable; the caller-facing variant keeps the blunt 32+ character rule. This also covers the MCP client's upstream error bodies, which are logged and were not edited here.

Upstream error text (d5). Stripe's error text reached the buyer at checkout (the seller's key state and its last four characters): it now goes to the log, redacted, and the buyer gets a plain sentence; only a card_error, which Stripe writes for the cardholder, passes. The e-invoicing operator's error and ack bodies reached every owner who sent an invoice, where a gateway that echoes the bearer would hand over the node's operator key: they go to the log, and the sender gets a sentence.

500 answers (d4). 75 route handlers answered a 500 with err.message or String(err), including the public federation routes. A new middleware, src/middleware/internal-error-text.ts, wraps res.json after systemFaultReporter: a 500 whose code means the node failed (message-audience 'ours': INTERNAL_ERROR, INTERNAL, *_FAILED, *_ERROR, *_TIMEOUT) gets a sentence that names the request id, and the original text goes to the log under the same id. All 75 sites carry such a code, so all are covered without editing them. 502, 503 and 504 keep their authored answers, and a route marks a 500 sentence it wrote for the caller with keepErrorMessage (settlement failed, login link failed, typed commerce errors, an extension script's own error, redacted). The fault report receives the sentence the caller saw and redacts what it forwards.

Idempotency cache (1.8). The cache kept the whole response for 24 hours, so a replay with the same Idempotency-Key handed a one-time secret out again (SCIM token, PAT, agent keys, TOTP secret and backup codes). A response marked Cache-Control: no-store, or one that carries a credential field, is no longer kept: the reservation stays, and a replay is answered 409 IDEMPOTENCY_RESULT_UNAVAILABLE, the protocol's answer for a response that is not available.

Admin backup (1.9). GET /v1/admin/backup spread whole agent rows, so every agent's plaintext webhook secret was in the file. Owners and agents are now written through an allowlist (src/services/admin-backup-projection.ts), agent memory leaves out credential records and share password hashes, and the response lists what it omitted. openapi.yaml says the same.

Tests that failed on the code before: test/unit/logger-redaction.test.ts (31 of 37), test/unit/upstream-error-text.test.ts (5 of 6), test/unit/internal-error-text.test.ts (the fault report redaction), test/unit/idempotency.test.ts (7 new), e2e-federation (a public 500 carried "TypeError: keyword.toLowerCase is not a function"), e2e-scim-users and e2e-access-tokens (the replay carried the token again, 201), e2e-agent-webhook 3b (the webhook secret was in the backup).

feat(docsign): sign a PDF with an EU Digital Identity Wallet

A party to a signing request can sign its PDF in an EU Digital Identity Wallet. The node is the relying party: the wallet makes the PAdES signature through its own trust service provider, so the node needs no account at a signature provider. Today it speaks the pre-standard "Document Retrieval" flow that the released EU reference wallet (Android) handles: an eudi-rqes:// link names a request object (a JWS signed with the node's relying-party access certificate, client_id_scheme x509_san_dns), the wallet downloads the PDF, signs and posts it back as a form. The protocol is kept to services/docsign/eudi.ts, so the ETSI TS 119 432 interface national wallets will speak becomes a second adapter beside it.

The node checks that the returned PDF begins with the exact bytes it sent and that the new signature verifies, stores the signed PDF in the signer's own files, and seals the signature into the request with method eudi-wallet (records.ts, sealing now shared by every method). A later wallet signer signs the newest signed PDF, so every signature lands in one file, which any party reads through GET /v1/docsign/requests/:id/signed-document (through the classification reader). The PDF is held in process memory for one 15-minute session only; the request still keeps hashes.

The EU reference wallet's test CAs (src/data/eudi-test-roots.ts, 14 public certificates) are trust anchors while docsign.eudi_test_roots is on; a signature under one is reported with TEST_TRUST_ANCHOR, trust source eudi-test-anchor and level unknown, never as qualified.

Routes in routes/docsign-wallet.ts (GET /v1/docsign/wallet, POST /v1/docsign/requests/:id/wallet, GET /v1/docsign/requests/:id/wallet/:session, GET /v1/docsign/requests/:id/signed-document, and the three wallet endpoints under /v1/docsign/wallet/:session/), with openapi. MCP tools aimeat_docsign_wallet_start and aimeat_docsign_wallet_status on all three surfaces. Settings docsign.eudi_enabled (off by default), docsign.eudi_rp_credential (a PEM file, set at start) and docsign.eudi_test_roots. The global form parser skips the wallet's response path, which its route parses at the signing size limit.

Tests: e2e-docsign plays the wallet (request object signature and host name checked as a wallet does, PDF downloaded, a PAdES signature appended) with six new cases, refusals included: a stranger, another PDF, a non-PDF, a wrong state, a returned PDF that is not the one sent, the original after a wallet signature. 23/23 on SQLite and Postgres. Unit: the response form variants and the test CAs. The fixture builders moved to test/fixtures/docsign/pdf-sign.ts, and eudi-rp-test.txt is a TEST-ONLY access credential naming localhost for the E2E node.

test(crewai): the decide feature, against a real node

Everything so far was offline plus one live call made by hand. A feature nobody can re-verify is a
feature that quietly rots, so this is the same ground as a pytest file anyone can run.

Real node process, real database, real decide service, real scrubber, real rule store, real gate,
real register, and the package's own public functions calling all of it over REST. 19 tests, and
the ones that matter are the ones an offline test cannot reach: a minted tool making a recorded
decision; STATE_OUTSIDE_RULE and RULE_FIXES_QUESTIONS refused by the NODE rather than by this
client, because the guarantee has to hold for any caller; the node's gate answering proceed:false
AND the held decision actually turning up on the owner's open-items list; a person's override
landing on the record; and the quality numbers counting that gate stop and that override.

TYPESAFE IS THE ONE STAND-IN, and it has to be. A suite that spends real money every time it runs
is a suite nobody runs, and assertions pinned to a live model's answers would be flaky for reasons
that have nothing to do with this code. JevStub speaks Jev's wire shape on loopback, and setting
its answers is what makes the interesting cases testable at all -- an outcome under the act band, a
missed threshold, a gate that holds -- because against a live model those are whatever it happens
to think today.

It is a SERVER rather than a mock on purpose: that is what lets a test assert what actually LEFT
the node. Only the fields the rule names, the owner's questions rather than the caller's, the
owner's key rather than the agent's, the pinned model id, and -- the one I would not have trusted
on reading alone -- that the scrubber really did remove an e-mail address and a phone number from
the body on the way out. A mock inside the process cannot see any of that, because by then it has
already gone.

The file skips itself unless aimeat/node_modules is installed. test_serve_loopback.py does not
check that, and without it the node exits instantly and its nine tests report as ERRORs that read
like broken code rather than missing setup -- which is exactly how they read on this machine
earlier today.

The two crew.menu tests cover crewfive's code and importorskip on `crewaimeat`, so they run on a
fleet machine and skip in this repo's CI. Verified passing with crewfive on the path.

Verified by mutation, not just by being green: dropping the rule id from the payload, ignoring the
node's proceed:false, and pointing decision_stats at the plain decisions list each turn the file
red.

feat(decide): decision rules on the node, the per-agent gate, and a key per agent

A DECISION RULE is a named set of questions, thresholds and bands an owner writes once
(memory record decide.rules.<id>, reserved prefix, no new table) and an app or an agent then
runs by id. A call that names a rule sends only the state: questions, thresholds or bands sent
beside it are refused, a state field outside the rule's `sends` is refused, and the `use` lock
(agent | app | both) is enforced in the service, so REST, MCP and a run over many records all
get it. The answers are cut into an outcome: an answer under its threshold is `stop`, otherwise
the weakest certainty among the thresholded answers is cut by the bands into act, ask or stop.

The decision row learns the rule: rule, ruleVersion, outcome and keyScope columns on both
providers (Postgres 0080, SQLite safeAddColumn), list filters by rule and by principal, and
aiDecisionStats counts decisions, outcomes, gate stops, reviews and cost in the store. The owner's
try of a rule on its sample is recorded but is not one of the rule's decisions.

The gate is a per-agent switch (on | off | each rule's own default), off by default so a comparison
run can run unguarded. On, an outcome under the act band answers proceed:false and puts an item on
the owner's open-items list; off, the agent may proceed and the same outcome is recorded.

An agent proposes a rule and creates nothing: the proposal is validated as a rule is, lands on the
owner's open-items list, and the owner's press creates the rule.

A key per agent for both models (decide.apikey.agent.<name>, openrouter.apikey.agent.<name>),
encrypted, resolved agent key, owner key, node key, with the record saying which paid, and a
per-agent daily cap in the shape of the per-app cap. No door returns a key; for an agent that runs
its own calls elsewhere the record may name the environment variable.

Found on the way: decide.apikey was not on the credential list, so the generic memory doors
returned its ciphertext. It is now, with the per-agent key records, matched by prefix.

ai-completion.ts was 26 lines under the file cap: its usage-accounting group moved to
ai-usage-record.ts unchanged and is re-exported.

MCP on all three surfaces: `rule` on aimeat_decide, aimeat_decide_run and aimeat_decision_list;
aimeat_decide_rules; aimeat_decide_rule_propose. openapi.yaml in the same change.

E2E test/e2e-ai-decide.ts phases 7 to 10 (17 new checks, each seen failing first), 40 of 40 on
sqlite and postgres-kysely. Unit tests for the validator, the evaluator and the storage counts.

feat(decide): a decision provider beside the text one, with the scrubber in the node path (TARGET-080)

TypeSafe's Jev answers typed questions with probabilities and writes no text, so it is not a model
in the picker: it has its own route, its own key and its own record, and shares the money with the
text path (the daily budget, the per-app quota, the per-person allowance on the node's key, the
ledger).

- POST /v1/ai/decide, decision reads and review, runs over many records, owner settings.
- Every byte sent is scrubbed first (e-mail, phone, henkilötunnus, IBAN, street address, contact
  names, name fields), choice option names included; real names are put back into the answers.
- An app must name TypeSafe in its data map before the node sends its data.
- One decision record per call in ai_decisions, beside ai_provenance; it doubles as the cache.
- Pinned model id, limits as configuration, retries as the TypeSafe SDKs do them.
- MCP on all three surfaces; no tool changes the settings.
